summary: Specifies the Point-to-Point Tunneling Protocol, which lets PPP traffic be tunneled through an IP network. It is informational and not a standard.

eli5.summary: A way to put one network's messages inside another's, like mailing a letter inside a bigger envelope that travels a different route.

questions: how does point to point tunneling work
what is a pac and pns in pptp
subtitle: How PPP dial-up sessions were carried across an IP network, with a TCP control channel and an enhanced GRE data tunnel.

tldr.problem: Traditional network access servers do everything in one box: answer the phone line, run PPP and route traffic. That ties dial-in users to one device and makes multilink bundles and private addressing awkward.
tldr.mechanism: PPTP splits the work between a PPTP Access Concentrator (PAC) and a PPTP Network Server (PNS). A TCP connection on port 1723 carries call control messages, and PPP packets travel between them inside enhanced GRE packets over IP.
tldr.outcome: PPP can run unchanged over an IP network, but the RFC itself warns that control messages and tunnel packets are not authenticated or cryptographically protected. It is an Informational memo, not a standard.

facts.label: User data MTU
facts.value: 1532 octets, not including IP and GRE headers

today: RFC 2637 is an Informational memo, not an Internet standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its own IESG note points to L2TP, then being defined by the PPP working group, as the Standards Track tunneling protocol (see RFC 2661).

sections.title: Splitting the Network Access Server
sections.content:
A network access server (NAS) traditionally handles the phone or ISDN line and modems, ends the PPP link, joins in PPP authentication, bundles channels for PPP Multilink, ends the PPP network control protocols and routes between its interfaces. PPTP divides these between two roles. The PAC (PPTP Access Concentrator) handles the line, PPP link termination and possibly authentication. The PNS (PPTP Network Server) runs on a general purpose server and handles multilink bundles, network control protocols and routing.

The RFC lists benefits: flexible IP address management, since dial-in users can keep one address while dialing into different PACs served by a common PNS. Non-IP protocols such as AppleTalk and IPX can be tunneled through an IP-only provider. And multilink channels may be spread across several PACs while one PNS handles the bundle.

Only the PAC and PNS need to know about PPTP, and standard PPP client software should keep working. PPTP can also tunnel a PPP session between two machines, with the caller acting as the PNS. The memo's IESG note says PPTP was developed by a vendor consortium and published for information, while the PPP working group was defining the Standards Track L2TP.
sections.eli5: One big helper used to do every job at the front door. PPTP gives the phone-answering job to one helper and the sorting-the-mail job to another, and they pass the mail through a tunnel.

sections.title: The Control Connection and Its Messages
sections.content:
Every PAC and PNS pair has a control connection, a plain TCP session opened to port 1723. Either side may open it. Each message starts with an 8-octet header holding the total length, the message type (1 for a control message, 2 for a management message, which is not yet defined) and a magic cookie, always 0x1A2B3C4D. Loss of synchronization with the TCP stream must close the control connection.

The RFC defines 15 control messages in four groups: connection management (Start-Control-Connection and Stop-Control-Connection requests and replies, plus Echo-Request and Echo-Reply), call management (Outgoing-Call and Incoming-Call messages, Call-Clear-Request and Call-Disconnect-Notify), error reporting (WAN-Error-Notify) and PPP session control (Set-Link-Info).

All data is in network order, and any reserved field MUST be sent as 0. The Start-Control-Connection messages carry a protocol version, whose current value is 0x0100 (version 1, revision 0), plus framing and bearer capabilities, a 64-octet host name and a 64-octet vendor string.
sections.eli5: Before the two helpers move any mail, they open a phone line and say hello. Every note starts with a secret stamp so the receiver knows it is a real PPTP note.

sections.title: Control Connection and Call Procedures
sections.content:
The side that first opens the TCP connection is the originator. It sends a Start-Control-Connection-Request, waits for the reply, and checks the version. If both sides open a connection at once, the peer with the higher IP address (compared as 32-bit unsigned values) wins. The loser closes its own TCP connection and answers the winner's request.

If no expected reply arrives within 60 seconds, the control connection is closed. An established connection that has seen no control message for 60 seconds SHOULD send an Echo-Request, and if no Echo-Reply comes within 60 seconds, the connection SHOULD be closed. A state transition that does not complete within 1 minute means the whole control connection should be closed and restarted, and all Call IDs are then released.

For an incoming call, the PAC sends an Incoming-Call-Request when the line rings, but does not answer. The PNS may refuse, for example when it has no resources or the caller is not authorized. If it accepts, it sends an Incoming-Call-Reply with window sizes, the PAC answers the call and sends Incoming-Call-Connected. The RFC calls this a three-way handshake. Each peer assigns a Call ID that MUST be unique for the tunnel, and a session is the triple (PAC, PNS, Call ID).
sections.eli5: The helpers keep checking that the line is still open by saying are-you-there every minute. When the phone rings, the first helper asks the second whether to pick up, and only picks up once the answer is yes.

sections.title: The Enhanced GRE Tunnel Header
sections.content:
User data travels as PPP packets, without media framing such as HDLC flags or CRCs, inside GRE packets over IP. PPTP uses a slightly enhanced GRE header with a new Acknowledgment Number field. The acknowledgments are not used to retransmit user data. They set the rate at which data is sent.

In the header, the K bit is set to one and the Ver field must be 1. The Protocol Type is hex 880B. The S bit is one when a payload is present, and the A bit is one when an acknowledgment number is present. The Key field is split: the high 2 octets are the payload length and the low 2 octets are the peer's Call ID, which tells the receiver which session the packet belongs to. The sequence number for each session starts at zero. The MTU for the encapsulated user packets is 1532 octets, not counting the IP and GRE headers.
sections.eli5: Each tunnel packet wears a label that says which phone call it belongs to and which packet number it is, so many calls can share one tunnel without getting mixed up.

sections.title: Flow Control with a Sliding Window
sections.content:
The tunnel uses a sliding window only for flow and congestion control. The peers never retransmit GRE packets. Each side states the maximum size of its receive window when the call is set up. The sender starts at half of that maximum, with a minimum of one packet, and stops when the number of unacknowledged packets equals the current window.

After each window is acknowledged without a time-out, the window grows by one packet up to the maximum. After a time-out it shrinks to half its size, rounded up, with a minimum of one. A single acknowledgment can cover several packets: all outstanding packets with a sequence number lower than or equal to the acknowledgment number are acknowledged.

Out-of-sequence packets MUST be silently discarded, though a receiver may instead reorder them, because PPP copes with loss but not with reordering. The RFC suggests, but does not require, an adaptive time-out in the style of the 1989 TCP algorithm, with gains of 1/8 for the average, 1/4 for the deviation and 4 for the time-out.
sections.eli5: Imagine passing buckets down a line. You start by sending a few, send more each time they all arrive safely, and slow down quickly if one goes missing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC leaves security of user data and authentication of the PPP peers to PPP itself. The PPTP control channel messages are neither authenticated nor integrity protected, so an attacker might hijack the underlying TCP connection, forge control messages, or alter genuine ones without detection.

The GRE packets forming the tunnel are not cryptographically protected either. Because PPP negotiation runs inside the tunnel, an attacker might eavesdrop on and modify it. Unless the PPP payload data is cryptographically protected, it can be captured, read or modified.
sections.eli5: The tunnel is like a clear plastic tube. Mail inside can be seen or swapped unless it was also locked in its own box before going in.

messages.label: Incoming-Call-Request
messages.note: The line rings; the PAC does not answer yet.

messages.label: Incoming-Call-Reply
messages.note: Accepts the call and gives window sizes.

messages.label: Incoming-Call-Connected
messages.note: The call is answered and both sides are established.

fields.name: C R K S s Recur A Flags
fields.desc: Flag bits; K is one, and S and A say whether data and an acknowledgment are present.

fields.name: Key (HW) Payload Length
fields.desc: Size of the payload, not including the GRE header.

fields.name: Key (LW) Call ID
fields.desc: The peer's Call ID for this session.

fields.name: Sequence Number (optional)
fields.desc: Sequence number of the payload, present if S is one.

fields.name: Acknowledgment Number (optional)
fields.desc: Highest sequence number received, present if A is one.

items.label: Outgoing-Call-Request
items.desc: Asks the PAC to place a call.

items.label: Incoming-Call-Reply
items.desc: PNS accepts or refuses the call.

items.label: Call-Clear-Request
items.desc: PNS asks to clear a call.

items.label: WAN-Error-Notify
items.desc: Reports errors on the PAC's WAN side.

items.label: Set-Link-Info
items.desc: Changes PPP link settings for a session.
